name: Smithfield Market
layers: Augustinian priory; jousting ground; public execution site; livestock market since 12th century; Victorian iron market hall still standing
narrative_notes: The ground beneath Smithfield is soaked in centuries of blood — animal and human alike. Wat Tyler's rebellion ended here; so did nearly 300 Protestant martyrs under Mary I. The fat of the executed is said to have made the cobblestones slick for days. The Victorian market hall sits atop a Norman priory like a lid on a reliquary.
drift_suggestion: Drift east toward the Charterhouse, a plague pit turned monastery turned school. The ground rises slightly — you are walking over the dead.

name: Fleet Street
key_dates: 43 AD (Roman road), 1500s (first printing presses), 1666 (Great Fire boundary), 1987 (newspapers depart)
layers: Roman road; medieval bridge over Fleet River; printing and journalism district; Sweeney Todd legend at St Clement Danes end
narrative_notes: The Fleet River runs beneath your feet, culverted and forgotten since 1765, still draining down to the Thames. You can sometimes hear it in the tunnels below Farringdon station. The newspaper district that roared here for five centuries fell silent in a single decade — the presses gone, the ghosts of ink and hot metal lingering in the sandstone.
drift_suggestion: Follow the course of the buried Fleet north toward Clerkenwell. The street dips slightly — that is the river valley, still holding its shape beneath the tarmac.

name: Aldgate
key_dates: 43 AD (Roman gate), 1374 (Chaucer lived above gate), 1665 (plague pit), 1888 (Ripper murders nearby)
layers: One of the original Roman gates of Londinium; Chaucer held the lease on the gatehouse room; plague pit beneath the junction; edge of the old Jewish quarter
narrative_notes: Chaucer wrote above this gate, listening to the creak of carts below. The Romans built the first arch here; it was demolished in 1761 and its stones sold for rubble. Beneath the roundabout lies one of the city's great plague pits — 1,000 bodies interred in a single week of 1665. You are standing on a palimpsest of thresholds.
drift_suggestion: Drift south into the old Minories — the street name echoes a convent of Franciscan nuns, dissolved by Henry VIII. The ghost of the precinct persists in the street grid.

name: Crossbones Graveyard
key_dates: Medieval (origins), 1853 (closed, overcrowded), 1996 (rediscovered during Jubilee Line works), 1998 (shrine established)
layers: Unconsecrated burial ground for Southwark's Winchester Geese (licensed prostitutes of the Bishop of Winchester); later paupers ground; over 15,000 bodies found during excavations
narrative_notes: The Bishop of Winchester licensed the brothels of Bankside and then denied their workers Christian burial. They were interred here, in unconsecrated ground, beyond the city walls and beyond mercy. The gate is covered in ribbons and tokens — a living shrine maintained by strangers. The geese got their graveyard back.
drift_suggestion: Walk west along Union Street toward the ruins of Winchester Palace — the great hall of the bishop who profited from the women buried behind you. The rose window still stands.

name: Newgate Prison
key_dates: 1188 (first prison), 1783 (Tyburn hangings moved here), 1868 (last public execution), 1902 (demolished, Old Bailey built)
layers: City gate turned debtors prison turned execution site; 1,169 public hangings outside its walls between 1783-1868; site now occupied by the Old Bailey
narrative_notes: The Old Bailey stands on the footprint of one of England's most notorious prisons. The condemned were walked from the cells to the scaffold outside — the route called the long walk was eleven steps. Dickens watched executions here and never recovered from what he saw. The street stones were relaid but the slope of the old ditch persists in the camber of the road.
drift_suggestion: Cross toward St Sepulchre-without-Newgate — the church bell was rung outside the condemned cell the night before execution. The handbell used for the ceremony is still kept inside.

name: Bunhill Fields
key_dates: 1549 (bones from St Paul's charnel house deposited), 1665 (plague overflow), 1713 (closed to new burials)
layers: Nonconformist burial ground; graves of William Blake, John Bunyan, Daniel Defoe; 123,000 bodies interred; never consecrated; name derives from Bone Hill
narrative_notes: William Blake was buried here in an unmarked grave — the exact spot uncertain, a stone placed nearby by guesswork. Defoe and Bunyan lie close. The plane trees are old enough to have shaded their funerals. This is the dissenter's city, the city that refused the established church, packed into a few acres of north London clay.
drift_suggestion: Drift west toward Moorfields — the Roman wall ran just south of here. Blake claimed to see angels in the trees of this neighbourhood as a child. Look up.

name: Tyburn
key_dates: 1196 (first recorded execution), 1571 (Tyburn Tree erected, triple gallows), 1783 (gallows removed, executions moved to Newgate)
layers: Principal place of execution for Middlesex for nearly 600 years; site now marked by a small plaque on a traffic island at Marble Arch; Tyburn River runs beneath
narrative_notes: The most famous execution ground in England is now a traffic island. A small brass plaque marks where the Tyburn Tree stood — a triangular gallows capable of hanging 24 people simultaneously. 50,000 people may have died here over six centuries. The Tyburn River, which gave the place its name, still flows beneath the road, joining the Thames near Vauxhall Bridge.
drift_suggestion: Follow the line of the old Oxford Road east — this was the route the condemned carts took from Newgate, a three-mile procession that took three hours through the crowds. You are walking the hangman's road.

name: St Giles-in-the-Fields
key_dates: 1101 (leper hospital founded), 1665 (plague pit, worst mortality in London), 1751 (Hogarth's Gin Lane set here)
layers: Former leper colony on the road out of London; bowl of ale given to condemned on the Tyburn procession; Seven Dials rookery; Hogarth's most savage satire
narrative_notes: Lepers gathered at this crossroads, ringing bells to warn travellers. By the 17th century it was a rookery — one of the most densely packed slums in Europe. Hogarth drew Gin Lane here: the woman dropping her baby, the pawnbroker's queue, the bodies in the street. The church watched over all of it from behind its Baroque portico.
drift_suggestion: Walk to Seven Dials — the column at the centre was rumoured to hide treasure and was torn down by a mob in 1773. It was rebuilt in 1989. Count the dials: there are seven sundials for seven streets.

name: Queenhithe
key_dates: 50 AD (Roman harbour), 899 AD (Alfred the Great develops dock), 1973 (dock closed)
layers: Oldest dock in London; Saxon harbour built by Alfred the Great; the last working dock in the upper Pool of London; mosaic on the wharf marks its history
narrative_notes: Queenhithe is a hollow in the north bank of the Thames — a Roman inlet that Alfred the Great shaped into a Saxon harbour. For a thousand years, grain and fish came ashore here. The wharf is quiet now, the cobbles worn smooth, a mosaic set into the ground by the city as an apology for forgetting. Stand at the edge and look at the river: the Saxons saw exactly this bend.
drift_suggestion: Walk east along the riverside to the site of the old Steelyard — the Hanseatic League's London headquarters for 400 years, demolished in 1863 for Cannon Street Station.

name: Moorgate
layers: Gate through the Roman wall leading to Moorfields; the moor beyond was used for archery, skating in winter, and was a favoured duelling ground; 1974 crash killed 43
narrative_notes: The gate is gone but the wall persists in fragments — visible in the basement of a nearby office block, in the curve of London Wall street, in the slight ridge in the pavement where the Roman ditch was filled. In 1974, a tube train failed to stop at Moorgate station and drove into the tunnel wall at 35mph. It remains the worst peace-time rail crash in British history.
drift_suggestion: Drift north along Coleman Street — during the Civil War this street was a stronghold of Parliamentarian dissent. Cromwell's London.

name: Execution Dock
layers: Admiralty gallows at the low-water mark; pirates and mutineers hanged and left for three tides; Captain Kidd's body left in a gibbet cage for two years as a warning to sailors
narrative_notes: The gallows stood at the low-water mark — Admiralty jurisdiction began where the Thames began, and so did Admiralty justice. Pirates were hanged here and left until three tides had washed over them. Captain Kidd's tarred body swung in a cage over the river for two years. The pub nearby is still called The Prospect of Whitby — smugglers drank there while the bodies dripped.
drift_suggestion: Drift east along Wapping High Street — the warehouses that line it held the wealth of empire. Now they are flats.

name: The Charterhouse
key_dates: 1348 (plague pit), 1371 (Carthusian monastery founded), 1537 (prior executed, monks dispersed), 1611 (almshouse founded)
layers: Plague pit beneath the cloister; Carthusian monastery dissolved by Henry VIII after its prior was hanged drawn and quartered; now almshouse and museum; parts of the cloister survive
narrative_notes: The Charterhouse was built over a plague pit — 50,000 bodies beneath the courtyard, interred in three months of 1348. The Carthusians who came after knew this and chose it anyway. Prior Houghton was the first English martyr of the Reformation, executed with maximum brutality at Tyburn. His arm was nailed to the monastery gate as a warning to the monks who remained.
drift_suggestion: Walk south toward Smithfield — you are retracing the cart route that carried Prior Houghton to his death. The distance is eight minutes on foot.

name: Greenwich Hill
key_dates: 43 AD (Roman temple on hill), 1427 (palace built below), 1675 (Royal Observatory founded), 1884 (Prime Meridian established)
layers: Roman temple at the summit; Tudor palace birthplace of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I; Wren's Observatory straddles the Prime Meridian; the hill is a natural ley point
narrative_notes: The Prime Meridian is an act of imperial imagination — a line drawn through a hilltop in south-east London and declared the centre of the world. Beneath the Observatory, a Roman temple occupied the same commanding position two thousand years earlier. The hill has always been a place from which power looks outward. Stand on the meridian line: one foot in the eastern hemisphere, one in the west.
drift_suggestion: Drift down through the park toward the Queen's House — Inigo Jones's white cube, the first purely classical building in England. It looks like it landed from another century.

name: Aldwych
key_dates: 600 AD (Saxon settlement), 1905 (Strand demolished for new crescent), 1994 (Aldwych tube station closed)
layers: Saxon settlement outside the Roman walls; the Strand follows the Saxon riverside path; Aldwych tube station closed 1994 and used as a film location; two churches by Wren marooned in the crescent
narrative_notes: Aldwych means old settlement in Old English — the Saxons built outside the abandoned Roman walls, along the river, following paths the Romans had not made. The 1905 crescent erased the medieval street pattern in one act of Edwardian surgery. The two Wren churches — St Clement Danes and St Mary le Strand — stand in the traffic like survivors of a flood.
drift_suggestion: Walk west along the Strand — the road follows the Saxon path so precisely that its curves are echoes of a riverbank that has not existed for 900 years.

name: The Monument
key_dates: 1666 (Great Fire begins at Pudding Lane, 2 September), 1677 (Monument completed by Wren)
layers: Wren's column marking the start of the Great Fire; height equals exact distance to bakery on Pudding Lane where fire began; 311 steps to the viewing platform; 13,200 houses destroyed
narrative_notes: The Monument is 202 feet tall. It stands 202 feet from the bakery on Pudding Lane where the fire started at 1am on 2 September 1666. This is either a remarkable coincidence or Wren's quiet joke. The fire burned for four days and destroyed four-fifths of the City. Only eight people are recorded as having died — almost certainly a significant undercount of the poor and the unrecorded.
drift_suggestion: Drift north to Pudding Lane — the bakery is gone, replaced by an office block. A plaque on the wall. The lane still runs, narrow and unremarkable, toward the church of St Magnus the Martyr.
